import/chips.add_cta:
Add one strong specific CTA at the very end of this content. The CTA must be specific to this content, not generic. Not 'what do you think' or 'let me know in the comments'. Ask a specific question tied to the content's main point, or direct to a specific action the reader can take today.

How to write it: find the single main point of the content, then ask the reader to answer a question about their own situation on that point, or to take one small named step (try a specific thing, check a specific item, reply with a specific answer). Match the platform's native CTA style and the brand voice. One CTA only; if the content already ends with a weaker CTA, replace it. Leave everything before the CTA unchanged. Do not add links, offers, prices or deadlines that are not already in the content or brand facts. Keep the language of the content. No em dashes.

GOOD: a question that only makes sense for this content ("Which step in your own week would you drop first?").
WEAK: "Thoughts? Let me know below."
import/chips.add_hashtags:
Add relevant brand-appropriate hashtags at the very end of this content. Use brand vocabulary and topic-specific terms. Never use generic hashtags like #motivation #success #hustle. LinkedIn: exactly 3 hashtags on a new line. Instagram: 8-10 hashtags after two blank lines. Twitter: 1 hashtag maximum only if it adds genuine context.

How to choose them: take the main topic, the audience and the brand's own terms from the content, then pick tags a real person in that niche would search or follow. For Instagram mix a few broader tags with several niche ones; for LinkedIn pick three that describe the topic precisely. Write each tag as one word or a short CamelCase phrase with no spaces, in the language of the content where a native tag exists. Do not change the content above the hashtags. Do not repeat a tag. Do not put hashtags inside the body text. No em dashes.

GOOD: tags that name the specific subject of this post.
WEAK: tags that could sit under any post in any industry.
import/chips.add_keywords:
Add 3-5 relevant SEO keywords naturally into this content. Keywords must fit the sentence structure, never forced or awkward. Do not list keywords separately. Weave them into existing sentences where they read naturally.

How to choose them: pick the phrases a reader would type into a search box to find this exact content (specific topic phrases, not single broad words). Place the most important one in the opening lines and the others in sentences where they are the natural wording. Reword only the sentences you need to; keep the meaning, the facts, the voice and the structure unchanged. Never repeat a keyword so often that it reads as stuffing, and never add a keyword the content does not actually cover. Keep the language of the content. No em dashes.

GOOD: "a weekly review for freelance designers" replacing "a weekly review" where the content is about that.
WEAK: a trailing line of keywords, or the same phrase in every paragraph.
import/chips.add_numbers:
Make vague claims in this content concrete. Use a number only if it already appears in the content or the brand facts, or can be counted from them. Do not invent statistics, prices, timeframes or quantities. If there is no real number to use, describe the outcome in plain, specific words instead and leave the numbers out.

How to do it: scan for vague words and claims (many, a lot, quickly, big improvement) and ask whether the content or brand facts support a real figure. If yes, state it exactly as given. If you can count something visibly in the text (for example the steps listed), you may state that count. If not, replace the vague claim with a concrete description of what happens, who it happens to, or what the reader would see. Keep the rest of the content, the voice and the language unchanged. No approximations such as "roughly" or "nearly half" unless the source says so. No em dashes.

GOOD: "The checklist has five steps" when five steps are listed; or "the team stopped rewriting captions by hand" when no number exists.
WEAK: a percentage saving that appears nowhere in the source.
import/chips.add_story:
Add a specific example to this content. Use only a real example that appears in the content or the brand facts. Do not invent a named person, a customer, a date, a number or something that supposedly happened. If there is no real example, illustrate the point with a short scenario introduced with Imagine or Picture so it reads as an illustration, not as a true event. Weave it into the existing content rather than appending it. No invented statistics.

How to do it: find the claim in the content that is most abstract, and place the example directly after it so it proves that claim. Keep the scenario to 2 to 4 sentences, with practical detail (what the person does, sees or decides) rather than a result with numbers. Keep the brand voice and the language of the content. Do not change the hook or the closing. No em dashes.

GOOD: "Imagine a freelancer who opens her inbox on Monday and sees three half-finished replies."
WEAK: a named client who supposedly reported a result with a number. That is invented.
import/chips.add_timestamps:
Add a timestamps section at the end of this content. Format each timestamp as: 00:00 Section Name. Create 4-6 logical sections based on the content structure. Start at 00:00. Space sections approximately evenly. Add [ADJUST TIMESTAMPS] note after the section.

How to do it: read the content in order and name each section after what it actually covers, using a short specific label of 2 to 6 words (not "Intro" and "Part 2" unless nothing better fits). Use real timestamps if the content already contains them; otherwise estimate even spacing and let the [ADJUST TIMESTAMPS] note tell the creator to correct them. Put one timestamp per line, in ascending order. Leave the existing content unchanged above the new section. Write labels in the language of the content. No em dashes.

GOOD: "03:10 Why the first draft fails"
WEAK: "03:10 Main part"
import/chips.expand:
Expand this content with more specific detail and depth. Add concrete examples drawn from the content or the brand facts, or a short scenario written in the content's own language (never as the opening line). Do not add numbers, names, dates or events that are not already in the content or the brand facts. Do not pad with generic observations. Every added sentence must contain a specific detail that only applies to this brand and this content. Target 50% more words than the original.

How to do it: for each main point, add the reason it is true, what it looks like in practice, or the objection a skeptical reader would raise and the answer to it. Keep the original hook, structure, voice and closing; add to the middle. Respect the platform's length limits and format if they are stated elsewhere in the prompt. Keep the language of the content. No em dashes.

GOOD: a sentence explaining what the reader would notice on their first day of trying the idea.
WEAK: "This is important because it really matters for success."
import/chips.fix_weasel_words:
Find the vague words in this content (many, several, often, recently, significant, various) and replace each with the real value only when the content or brand facts give it, or with the actual items for "various". If the real value is not known, restructure the sentence so it needs none. Never invent statistics.

How to do it: also catch similar hedges (some, a lot, a few, quite, really, very, fairly, huge, soon). For each one, check whether the content or brand facts give the real value. If they do, state it. If they do not, rewrite the sentence so it makes a plain specific statement without the hedge (name the actual items, the actual action or the actual outcome), or remove the hedge if the sentence still stands. Change only what is needed; keep the structure, voice, facts and language. No em dashes.

GOOD: "various tools" becomes "the scheduler, the editor and the inbox" when the content names them.
WEAK: "many" becomes a percentage that has no source.
import/chips.make_punchier:
Rewrite this content with shorter sentences. Cut every word that does not pull its weight. Bold statements. High energy. No filler. Maximum 2 sentences per paragraph. Do not add new ideas, sharpen what is already there.

How to do it: replace weak verb phrases with strong single verbs, delete qualifiers (very, really, just, kind of), lead each sentence with its subject and action, and cut throat-clearing openers. Keep every specific detail, name and number that exists; keep the meaning, the CTA and the language. Vary sentence length a little so it does not become monotonous. Do not turn it into a list unless it was one. No em dashes.

GOOD: "We stopped guessing. We tracked it."
WEAK: "We have actually really started to try to track things instead of guessing."
import/chips.more_casual:
Rewrite in a more conversational friendly tone. Use contractions. Shorter sentences. Sound like a knowledgeable friend talking, not a company presenting. Keep all the specific details and numbers.

How to do it: swap formal vocabulary for everyday words, address the reader as "you", allow a natural aside or a short fragment where a person would speak that way, and drop corporate phrases (leverage, utilise, solutions). Keep the facts, the structure, the CTA and the brand's banned and preferred words exactly as they are. Do not add slang that does not suit the brand or the audience, and do not add emojis unless the content already uses them. Keep the language of the content and use that language's natural informal register (contractions where the language has them). No em dashes.

GOOD: "Here's the thing most people skip."
WEAK: "It is recommended that individuals consider the following."
import/chips.more_formal:
Rewrite in a more formal professional tone. Complete sentences. No contractions. Structured and authoritative. Keep all the specific details and numbers.

How to do it: use precise vocabulary, a clear order (claim, reason, implication), and measured confidence rather than hype. Remove slang, fragments, exclamation marks and emojis. Keep the facts, the hook idea, the CTA and the brand's banned and preferred words exactly as they are. Do not make it longer with filler or stiff phrasing; formal does not mean wordy. Keep the language of the content and use that language's formal register. No em dashes.

GOOD: "The review should be completed weekly so that issues surface early."
WEAK: "It is of paramount importance to endeavour to utilise synergistic best practices."
import/chips.shorten:
Cut this content to approximately half its current length. Keep only the strongest sentences, the ones with specific details or real tension. Every removed sentence should disappear entirely, not be summarised. Never cut the hook or the closing. Cut from the middle.

How to choose what stays: keep sentences with a concrete detail, a name, a number from the source, or a turn in the argument. Remove repeated points, background, restated claims and transitions. After cutting, read it once through and fix any joins so it still flows, without adding new content. Keep the format, voice, language and CTA. Respect the platform's minimum length if one is stated elsewhere in the prompt. No em dashes.

GOOD: the hook, the two most specific points, the closing.
WEAK: every paragraph kept with each sentence shortened.
import/chips.simplify_show_notes:
Rewrite this content as clean podcast show notes. Remove complex sentences. Short paragraphs of 2-3 sentences. Scannable structure with clear section breaks. End with a specific listener takeaway or action.

Structure: a one-line headline stating what the episode delivers, a 2 to 3 sentence summary, short labelled sections or bullets for the main ideas (each naming a concrete idea or example), any standout quote exactly as it appears, and a closing takeaway. Use plain words and active voice. Keep only details that are already in the content: do not invent guests, links, timestamps, numbers or quotes. Keep the language of the content. No em dashes.

GOOD: "The host explains why a short weekly review beats a long monthly one."
WEAK: "A great discussion with many insights."
import/chips.stronger_hook:
Rewrite ONLY the opening line to be more specific and scroll-stopping. Lead with a concrete detail from the content below, a real number, a named moment, or an observation the reader feels but rarely sees said out loud, whichever fits this content best. Do not default to the same structure every time this instruction runs. Keep the rest of the content completely unchanged. The new hook must not start with: Are you, Many people, Most people, In today's world, We all know, Did you know, Imagine, Picture this, The uncomfortable truth. Two punchy sentences maximum.

How to do it: find the most surprising, specific or tense point in the content and say it directly in the first line. Use a number or named moment only if it already appears in the content or brand facts. The hook must be true to the rest of the content and must lead naturally into the second line as it stands. Match the brand voice and the language of the content. Return the full content with only the first line replaced. No em dashes.

GOOD: a first line that states the one decision or mistake the post is about.
WEAK: a question that could open any post on the topic.

import/text_engagement:
HIGH-PERFORMING HOOK PATTERNS — pick whichever structure best fits THIS
piece's actual content; do not default to the same one every time. Every
pattern below is a structural description to paraphrase in your own words,
in the brand's own voice — none of them is a phrase to reuse or fill in
like a template:

1. Contrarian stat: open by naming a common belief, then contradict it with
   a real detail from the source content.
2. Specific outcome: open with a concrete result or number from the source
   content, then reveal what actually caused it.
3. Pattern interrupt: open mid-story, from inside a real experience, then
   name the thing about it nobody usually says out loud.
4. Failed assumption: open with an assumption the author used to hold, then
   the specific moment that broke it.
5. Named discomfort: open by naming a true but rarely-said observation, then
   explain the real reason behind it, not the polite excuse people give.

BODY RULES:
- Every paragraph = 1-2 sentences maximum
- Every claim needs a concrete example within the same sentence, drawn from
  the brand's own story or the source content — never an invented number
- No adjective without evidence:
    ✗ "powerful tool" → ✓ "the tool I built after the third client asked for the same fix"
    ✗ "significant results" → ✓ "the exact thing that changed once we stopped doing X"
- No vague timelines:
    ✗ "recently" → ✓ the real day or moment named in the source; if the source names none, leave the timeline out
    ✗ "often" → ✓ a specific real instance from the source content

CLOSING RULES:
- End with a specific action, specific question, or specific next step
- Never end with motivation ("you can do this!")
- End with utility:
    ✓ "Try this with your next post. Tell me what breaks."
    ✓ "Open your budget this Sunday. Notice the one number that surprises you."
    ✓ "What is the first thing you would cut if you saw your spending snapshot?"
import/text_specificity:
OUTPUT STANDARD — NON-NEGOTIABLE:

BANNED OPENINGS — never start with any of these:
✗ "In today's world" / "In today's fast-paced world"
✗ "Are you tired of" / "Have you ever wondered"
✗ "We all know" / "It's no secret" / "Everyone knows"
✗ "I am excited to share" / "Thrilled to announce"
✗ "As a [profession]" / "As someone who"
✗ "The uncomfortable truth" / "An uncomfortable truth" — this default has
  been overused; if this angle genuinely fits, open with the specific
  observation itself instead of the label

BANNED CLOSINGS — never end with any of these:
✗ "So, are you ready to" / "The choice is yours"
✗ "What are you waiting for" / "Don't hesitate to"
✗ "The future is now" / "Join us on this journey"
✗ "You've got this" / "I believe in you"
✗ "Let's connect" / "Feel free to reach out"

NO EM DASHES — THIS IS A HARD RULE:
✗ NEVER use the em dash character (—) anywhere in the output
✓ Use a period, comma, or a plain word ("and", "but", "so") instead

NO INVENTED FACTS — THE MOST IMPORTANT RULE:
Everything the piece states as having happened or as a number must be in the source content or the brand facts above:
✗ NEVER invent a test, a client, a call, a project, a result, a date ("last Thursday"), a price, a score or a percentage
✗ NEVER write "I ran a test", "a customer told me", "we saw 40%" unless the source says so
✓ First person is for beliefs, opinions and how the product works, not for events that are not in the source
✓ To illustrate a point without a real example, introduce it as a scenario: "Imagine a team that..."
✓ If the source has too little real detail, keep every statement true and concrete, and reach the platform's minimum length with teaching, a scenario or a question for the reader, never with made-up detail

WRITE ADVICE, NOT A REPORT OF WHAT THE BRAND DID:
You do not know what this brand did last week, what its team tried, or what its customers said, unless the source says so. So the post teaches the reader. It does not narrate the brand's own history.
✗ NEVER write "our team", "we switched", "we closed", "in our case study", "our customers told us", "last week we", "a client of ours" unless the source says exactly that
✗ NEVER give a measured result: no "saved 30 minutes", "cut replies by half", "within a week the board showed". A result is a fact, and you have none
✓ Speak to the reader in the second person: "you", "your team", "if you"
✓ Teach with a general practice or a scenario: "Imagine a team that...", "A simple way to start is...", "For example, a small team could..."
✓ A time or a number is allowed only as a suggestion to the reader ("try ten minutes a day", "start with one board"), never as something that happened or was measured
✓ The most believable post is a clear idea, one concrete step the reader can take today, and one honest question

NO FABRICATED STATISTICS — THIS IS A HARD RULE:
✗ NEVER invent percentages, survey results, or third-party stats
✗ NEVER write "X% of marketers", "studies show", "research says" unless
  that exact stat appears in the source content provided
✗ NEVER approximate a stat ("roughly 70%", "nearly half") — if you don't
  have the real number, don't use a number
✓ Use the brand's own story and real outcomes instead, but only what the source or the brand facts above actually say (these lines only show the style):
    - "I built the system. Now I teach it."
    - "The people still posting two years in tend to batch their work." (say it as a belief, not as a measured fact)
✓ Specificity from the brand's real details beats invented research every time; if there is no real detail, say less
✓ One real story > five fabricated statistics

GOOD VS BAD EXAMPLES:

BAD:  "Are you tired of budgeting apps that don't work?"
GOOD: "You downloaded the budgeting app, set it up on a Sunday, and by Wednesday it was a tab you never opened."

BAD:  "In today's world, content creation is more challenging than ever."
GOOD: "You rewrite the same post three times before you notice the problem was the first line, not the idea."

BAD:  "So, are you ready to transform your finances?"
GOOD: "Try this on Sunday. Open your budget. Close it as soon as you have named one thing that surprised you. Tell me what it was."

BAD:  "We all know that consistency is key to success."
GOOD: "The habit that keeps a posting streak alive for years is batching: write several posts in one sitting."

BAD:  "70% of marketers lack a content strategy." (fabricated)
GOOD: "Build a system for your content, or the content will build a burnout for you."

BAD:  "Many people struggle with content consistency."
GOOD: "A stretch of daily posting, then a long silence, then the guilt that restarts the cycle."

RULE: Every sentence must earn its place with a specific detail from THIS brand's story.
- Use a number or an outcome only when the source or the brand facts above state it; never invent one, and never use "3x qualified leads" style claims otherwise
- Use real moments from the brand story. Without one, leave the time out: never make up a day or date
- Delete any sentence that could be published by any brand in any industry
